qa.q: Why does no schedule reach 90% of the optimum?
qa.a: The learners solve a fitted model whose DP solution is worth about 126.6 on the oracle model, against a rule value of 113.6 and an optimum of 144.9. They end near that solution (Q-learning 124.4, MC 117.3), so the target is out of reach for any schedule; the limit is the support of the logged data, not exploration.

qa.q: If exploration matters little, why is near greedy Q-learning slower?
qa.a: Near greedy Q-learning has a mean AUC of -0.16 against 0.29 for the best schedule, and a plausible reason (not tested separately) is that it tries few actions early and needs many steps to correct its initial values. That is a speed effect within a fixed model; its final value is within the range of the other schedules.

qa.q: Why are the learners so far ahead of the rule on real data?
qa.a: The rule books one or two extra patients, and with about 19% of patients not coming that leaves 44.3 idle slots per episode and a summed waiting list of 211. The learners book more in some states and cut the waiting list to 98 to 115.

qa.q: Can we conclude that exponential decay is best for Q-learning?
qa.a: No. Its return in the schedule study (169.5) differs by 2.5 from the same configuration in the benchmark (167.0), which is comparable to the 4.3 unit spread across all five Q-learning schedules, and the same schedule ranks 4 of 5 for MC.

qa.q: Is the robustness result a reason to deploy the learned policy?
qa.a: No. It is a change of a single quantity made by flipping recorded outcomes, scored on one period of real sessions. It shows that the learned policies lose less than the rule when no-shows rise, in all 10 of 10 configurations, and nothing more.

qa.q: Why does the oracle score more than the learners?
qa.a: With 1,500 episodes the high overbooking actions are supported (about 50 visits per pair against 5.0), and the oracle uses +3 or +4 in 12 states. The learners use them in at most 4.

qa.q: Why does the structured model score more than the oracle fitted to ten times as much data?
qa.a: The oracle still estimates P(s' | s, a) pair by pair, so with 1,500 days some pairs that the optimum uses remain below the support threshold and the rest carry sampling error. The structured model estimates 26 numbers that every logged session informs and computes the rest from the clinic's rules; its return varies by ±0.01 over 20 data draws.

qa.q: Is the comparison fair to the learners?
qa.a: They receive the same logged days, the same solver for DP and the same scoring episodes. What the structured model has in addition is the clinic's rules, which Section 9 lists as a limitation: a clinic that cannot state them cannot use it.

qa.q: Why is the margin over the single session optimiser so small?
qa.a: In the default setting the waiting list stays short under both policies (1.83 and 1.67 patients per session), so little is left to plan for, and the optimiser uses each patient's own risk while the structured model uses a band. When the waiting list is under pressure the margin reaches 33.3% (Table 9).

qa.q: Which parts of the results are real?
qa.a: Attendance is real: every patient in a scored session is a recorded appointment and comes exactly when the table says so, and the scoring weeks are never used for learning. The overbooking decisions in the logs, the waiting list and the reward weights are not in the table and are generated or assumed (Section 6.1).
